newsitem.title: USA: Coca-Cola down on currency fears - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola down on currency fears - analysts.

text.p: Coca-Cola Co shares fell five percent in early afternoon trading on Friday amid concerns foreign currency exposure could have more impact on the company's earnings than previously expected.

Coke issued a news release early Friday, saying it expected third quarter earnings slightly ahead of last year's level of $0.39 per share. The statement exposed latent concerns about the impact of foreign currency exchange, analysts said.
Coke's five percent decline amid a broad market decline was the sharpest among the 30 companies that make up the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
"I think the principal problem is the strong dollar," Prudential Securites analyst George Thompson said. "That came to the surface today."
Thompson noted that 40 percent of Coke's operating income comes from Germany and Japan.
Sandra Kim, an analyst at Smith Barney, said the problem potentially was even more severe in emerging markets, whose currencies are harder for the company to hedge.
Coke's fundamentals, however, remain strong, said Kim, who added that Friday's overall market decline probably was pulling the company down with it.
"They basically move with the market ... just because it's a core holding," she said.
Coke went from a stock price in the 50s in April to 72 in mid-June, and some who follow the stock may have decided that it got a little ahead of itself, Kim said.
"They've had a huge run," she said.
Coke was down 3-5/16 to 63-1/4 in the early afternoon.
The analysts said it was unlikely that Friday's report would spark lower near-term estimates for Coke. The First Call consensus estimate for the third quarter was $0.44 per share.

Thompson said that Coke's earnings reports tend to be confusing, including various charges and gains that make comparisons difficult. But he agreed that Coke's business fundamentals, including volume trends, are in good shape.
Coke reported Friday that it would record a gain of $0.04 to $0.06 per share in the third quarter from selling its stakes in two bottlers, but would report earnings "slightly higher" than a year ago.
That prompted some analysts to contact the company, and in the course of those conversations the currency issue was revisited, Thompson said.
"If the dollar stays strong, it's going to impact them," he said.

Coke's news release did not specifically mention the foreign currency issue. But it cautioned that structural change from its bottling strategy "may have short-term, periodic impact on reported results, including both positive and negative effects on revenues, operating income and net income."
